title: Cup with Handle
teaches: The cup with handle as we trade it: a leader that ran at least 30% rests in a smooth rounded U for seven weeks or more, climbs back near the old high, then dips into a quiet handle of five sessions or more that sits above the cup's midpoint, drifts down and holds the 50-day; the buy is the trade through the handle high at market in regular hours, the stop a few cents under the day's low and never past the handle low, a third off at 3R and 5R with the rest on the trail, and a loss taken at the stop is the plan working.

facts.quote: Cup-with-handle patterns are shaped like the silhouette of a tea cup viewed from the side.
facts.claim: IBD: a cup with handle is shaped like a tea cup seen from the side.

facts.quote: Cups should show smooth action on the left and right sides of the pattern.
facts.claim: IBD: both sides of a cup should be smooth.

facts.quote: There shouldn't be jagged edges or many wild weekly swings of 10% to 15% or more.
facts.claim: IBD: no jagged edges or many wild weekly swings of 10% to 15% or more.

facts.quote: V-shaped patterns are less reliable.
facts.claim: IBD: V-shaped patterns are less reliable.

facts.quote: The pattern's basic requirements start with a run up of at least 30% before the stock turns down into a consolidation.
facts.claim: IBD: the cup needs a run up of at least 30% before it.

facts.quote: A proper cup base needs to span a minimum of seven weeks, while a flat base can be as short as five weeks.
facts.claim: IBD: a cup spans at least seven weeks.

facts.quote: The base must be at least seven weeks long, including the handle.
facts.claim: IBD: at least seven weeks, the handle included.

facts.quote: They range from seven weeks to as long as 65 weeks in length, with many forming over three to six months.
facts.claim: IBD: cups run 7 to 65 weeks, many forming over three to six months.

facts.quote: The size of the decline, or correction, in a cup base should generally be between 12% and 33%.
facts.claim: IBD: a cup's decline is generally between 12% and 33%.

facts.quote: In bear markets, cups can run as deep as 50%.
facts.claim: IBD: in bear markets cups can run as deep as 50%.

facts.quote: to correct 1-1/2 to 2-1/2 times the market averages
facts.claim: IBD: a growth stock's cup corrects 1.5 to 2.5 times the market averages.

facts.quote: A proper handle forms in the upper half of a base and drifts slightly downward along its price lows.
facts.claim: IBD: a proper handle forms in the upper half and drifts slightly down along its lows.

facts.quote: In the handle, the midpoint of the handle's high and low marks should be above the midpoint of the high and low of the left side of the cup
facts.claim: IBD: the handle's midpoint sits above the cup's midpoint.

facts.quote: Handles that form too low present added risk of failure during breakouts.
facts.claim: IBD: handles that form too low fail more often.

facts.quote: Second, a handle should generally form above the 50-day or 10-week moving averages.
facts.claim: IBD: a handle generally forms above the 50-day line.

facts.quote: Handles must be at least five days long, and typically last for several weeks.
facts.claim: IBD: handles are at least five days long.

facts.quote: If it's shorter than five days, it's not a handle.
facts.claim: IBD: under five days it is not a handle.

facts.quote: Stocks with wedging handles have a higher failure rate and often are seen in late-stage bases
facts.claim: IBD: wedging handles fail more often and show up in late-stage bases.

facts.quote: Overeager handles that wedge upward tend to fail, while handles that drift lower foreshadow assertive action.
facts.claim: IBD: handles that wedge up tend to fail; handles that drift lower lead to strong moves.

facts.quote: A wedging handle with no shakeouts is a sign to steer clear.
facts.claim: IBD: a wedging handle with no shakeouts is a reason to stay away.

facts.quote: Volume should mostly ease until the breakout.
facts.claim: IBD: volume mostly eases until the breakout.

facts.quote: Volume should dry up, evidence that the weak holders are just about gone.
facts.claim: IBD: volume in the handle dries up as weak holders leave.

facts.quote: Handles should have areas of tight trading and days or weeks where volume contracts sharply.
facts.claim: IBD: handles show tight trading and sharp volume contraction.

facts.quote: The buy point is located by taking the highest price in the handle and adding 10 cents.
facts.claim: IBD's buy point is the handle's highest price plus 10 cents.

facts.quote: the rule says to sell all your shares of a stock if it falls 7% or 8% below the price at which you bought it.
facts.claim: IBD's general loss limit is 7% or 8% below the purchase price.

facts.quote: It's usually best to buy when a stock breaks out from a first-stage or second-stage base.
facts.claim: IBD: it is usually best to buy a first- or second-stage base.

facts.quote: Breakouts from late-stage bases will often blow up.
facts.claim: IBD: late-stage breakouts often blow up.

facts.quote: Once your stock has broken out, take most of your profits when they reach 20% to 25%.
facts.claim: IBD's general profit rule: take most profits at 20% to 25%.

facts.quote: The Cup & Handle is the corrective action after a powerful stock advance.
facts.claim: Zanger: the cup is the rest after a powerful advance.

facts.quote: The stock will sell off into the correction in a downward fashion for maybe 20 to 35 percent off the old high point.
facts.claim: Zanger: the cup falls maybe 20% to 35% off the old high.

facts.quote: The handle is generally about 5% below the old high point. A handle that is any lower is generally a defective stock and contains higher risk for failure.
facts.claim: Zanger: the handle sits about 5% below the old high; lower is riskier.

facts.quote: The time to buy the stock, is as it emerges into new highs at the top of the handle and not the old high point set some 8 to 12 weeks ago.
facts.claim: Zanger buys as it emerges into new highs at the top of the handle.

facts.quote: the best stocks with this formation are found at the beginning of a market move after a good market correction, and not during, or at the end of a major market advance.
facts.claim: Zanger: the best cups come at the start of a market move after a correction.

facts.quote: The cup should be U-shaped, not V-shaped, but allow variations.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: the cup is U-shaped, not V-shaped.

facts.quote: From 7 to 65 weeks (allow variations).
facts.claim: Bulkowski: a cup lasts 7 to 65 weeks.

facts.quote: 1 week minimum with no maximum, forming in the upper half of the cup.
facts.claim: Bulkowski: the handle lasts at least a week and forms in the upper half.

facts.quote: The handle low (point C) is a good place to put a stop. Raise the stop as price rises.
facts.claim: Bulkowski puts the stop at the handle low and raises it as price rises.

facts.quote: buy when price closes above the right cup rim
facts.claim: Bulkowski buys on a close above the right rim.

facts.quote: A V-shaped bottom would be considered too sharp of a reversal to qualify.
facts.claim: StockCharts: a V-shaped bottom is too sharp to qualify.

facts.quote: the handle should not extend into the lower half of the cup.
facts.claim: AAII: the handle should not reach into the lower half of the cup.

facts.quote: prices should have advanced at least 30% from the last intermediate low.
facts.claim: AAII: price should have advanced at least 30% from the last intermediate low.

facts.quote: Stop first (by default a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, F62); the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
facts.claim: A3: stop first, a few cents under the day's low; the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit, skip.

facts.quote: The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule (B20).
facts.claim: A4: the stop is the exit; it only moves up, never wider; the gap rule is the one exception.

facts.quote: Shares = account × risk % ÷ (entry − stop), rounded down, then capped: the size is the SMALLER of the risk-based size and the position cap
facts.claim: A5: shares are account times risk percent, divided by entry minus stop, rounded down, then capped.

facts.quote: "I almost never take a loss greater than 3%": the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy (a loss on the position, not the account).
facts.claim: A13: the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy.

facts.quote: Move the stop to breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally. The first trim: the hard rule is a third at 3R; ideally anywhere from 3R to 6R, and in practice he mostly waits for 5R.
facts.claim: B19: breakeven between 2R and 5R; the hard rule for the first trim is a third at 3R.

facts.quote: A gap against the stop: the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. The low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop.
facts.claim: B20: on a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop.

facts.quote: With a ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.
facts.claim: B20's ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.

facts.quote: No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report; hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R.
facts.claim: B22: no new buys in the 3 days before a report; hold through one only if up 5R.

facts.quote: No chasing: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.
facts.claim: C28: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.

facts.quote: Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink (A5).
facts.claim: C28: chasing costs size, because the stop stays put and the distance grows.

facts.quote: Too stretched to buy: skip a long that is more than 10% above its 10-day average.
facts.claim: C29: skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average.

facts.quote: After the first third at 3R: another third at 5R, then trail the last third; adjustable.
facts.claim: E51: another third at 5R, then trail the last third.

facts.quote: Default trail: the 10-day average for fast movers, the 21-day for steadier ones; sell on a close below it.
facts.claim: E52: trail the 10-day for fast movers, the 21-day for steadier ones; sell on a close below it.

facts.quote: Entries are market orders.
facts.claim: E57: entries are market orders.

facts.quote: No new buys outside regular trading hours.
facts.claim: E58: no new buys outside regular hours.

facts.quote: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it.
facts.claim: F62: the stop sits a few cents under the day's low.

facts.quote: The market reading as a guide (A10): Green, full risk per grade and up to 10 positions; Yellow, smaller and fewer; Orange, only A+ setups; Red, mostly cash and shorts.
facts.claim: F65: Green full risk; Yellow smaller and fewer; Orange only A+; Red mostly cash and shorts.

facts.quote: After a market correction, when the reading turns Green again, start with a few positions and add more only as the first ones work
facts.claim: F68: after a correction, start with a few positions and add as they work.

facts.quote: After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule.
facts.claim: B21: after a stop-out, buy again only on a new trigger, as a new trade.

facts.quote: Setup grades set the size: A and B setups at normal size; A+ sized up; B- or lower sized down.
facts.claim: D38: A and B normal size, A+ sized up, B- or lower sized down.

facts.quote: In a Red market: mostly cash, plus shorts below the 200-day.
facts.claim: D46: in a Red market, mostly cash plus shorts below the 200-day.

facts.quote: A climax run on your own long (Bracco's parabolic burst): sell a big part into it, a judgment call.
facts.claim: C34: sell a big part of a long into a climax run.

facts.quote: a 3-5 day final leg: three straight up days, two straight overnight gap ups, two of three days of range expansion, two days of rising volume, and a gap up on the climax day
facts.claim: B26: the parabolic burst is a 3 to 5 day final leg of up days, gaps, range expansion and rising volume.

facts.quote: Grading a setup (A+, A, B, B-) is discretionary and hard to define; no fixed checklist is taught as ours.
facts.claim: E50: grading is discretionary; no fixed checklist is ours.

facts.quote: The pivot is the highest price in the handle.
facts.claim: The pivot is the handle's highest price.

facts.quote: IBD adds 10 cents; with market orders the 10 cents does not matter.
facts.claim: IBD's 10 cents does not matter with a market order.

facts.quote: Price trades above the pivot during regular hours. Buy with a market order.
facts.claim: The trigger: price trades above the pivot in regular hours; buy at market.

facts.quote: The stock rose at least 30% from its lowest low of the prior 6 months (120 sessions) to the left-side high.
facts.claim: At least 30% from the lowest low of the prior 6 months to the left-side high.

facts.quote: At least 7 weeks (35 sessions) from the left-side high to the day before the breakout, the handle included.
facts.claim: At least 7 weeks, the handle included.

facts.quote: A rounded U, not a V: at least 30% of the cup's bars have their low in the cup's bottom quarter.
facts.claim: A rounded U: at least 30% of the cup's bars have lows in its bottom quarter.

facts.quote: At most two weeks inside the cup with a high-to-low range of 10% or more.
facts.claim: At most two weeks with a 10% or wider range inside the cup.

facts.quote: The right side climbs back to within about 10% of the left-side high before the handle starts.
facts.claim: The right side climbs back within about 10% of the left-side high before the handle.

facts.quote: The handle is at least 5 sessions long.
facts.claim: The handle is at least 5 sessions long.

facts.quote: The handle's midpoint (halfway between its high and low) sits above the cup's midpoint.
facts.claim: The handle's midpoint sits above the cup's midpoint.

facts.quote: The handle's lows drift sideways to down: a straight line fitted through the handle's daily lows slopes flat or down. Rising lows (a wedge) is not a handle.
facts.claim: The handle's lows drift sideways to down; rising lows are a wedge, not a handle.

facts.quote: The handle's average daily volume is below the cup's average daily volume.
facts.claim: The handle's volume averages below the cup's.

facts.quote: The handle holds above the 50-day line: no daily close below the 50-day SMA during the handle.
facts.claim: No daily close below the 50-day during the handle.

facts.quote: Tight at the end: the last 5 handle closes sit within about 3% of each other.
facts.claim: Tight at the end: the last 5 handle closes within about 3% of each other.

facts.quote: A few cents under the low of the buy day, or of the prior day.
facts.claim: The stop: a few cents under the buy day's low or the prior day's low.

facts.quote: Never wider than a few cents under the handle low: below the handle low the setup has failed. IBD's 7% to 8% loss limit is a reference, not ours.
facts.claim: Never wider than a few cents under the handle low; IBD's 7% to 8% is not ours.

facts.quote: 62% of cup breakouts come back to the breakout price within 30 days (Bulkowski). The day's-low stop will be tested often; that is normal, not a reason to widen it.
facts.claim: 62% of cup breakouts come back to the breakout price within 30 days; the stop is tested, not widened.

facts.quote: After the buy, a close back into the handle is a warning, not an exit by itself.
facts.claim: A close back into the handle is a warning, not an exit.

facts.quote: First or second base since the last real correction; a third or later base is graded down.
facts.claim: First or second base; a third or later is graded down.

facts.quote: Before the buy: the cup is a V, or deeper than 35% outside a bear market.
facts.claim: A V, or deeper than 35% outside a bear market, ends the setup.

facts.quote: Before the buy: the handle runs past about 6 weeks (30 sessions) with no breakout; the base is getting stale.
facts.claim: A handle past about 30 sessions with no breakout is stale.

facts.quote: Before the buy: volume rises through the handle.
facts.claim: Volume rising through the handle ends the setup.

facts.quote: Before the buy: a close below the 50-day during the handle.
facts.claim: A close below the 50-day during the handle ends the setup.

facts.quote: Before the buy: the handle's lows rise (wedging), or the handle is shorter than 5 days.
facts.claim: Rising handle lows, or a handle under 5 days, end the setup.

facts.quote: Up to 50% deep only for a cup formed in a bear market.
facts.claim: Up to 50% deep only in a bear market.

facts.quote: The cup falls no more than about 2.5 times the index's decline over the same weeks.
facts.claim: The cup falls no more than about 2.5 times the index's decline.

facts.quote: A cue, not a rule: best at the start of a new market uptrend after a correction, with the group leading and several of its stocks setting up.
facts.claim: Best at the start of a new uptrend, with the group leading.

facts.quote: A flat base falls 15% or less and stays boxy with a flat ceiling tapped at least twice; a cup falls 12% to 33% in a rounded U and then dips again into a handle before the buy.
facts.claim: A flat base stays boxy; a cup is a deeper rounded U followed by a handle.

facts.quote: A cup is one rounded decline whose right side climbs back within 10% of the old high, then one handle at the rim; a VCP shows two or more separate pullbacks, each smaller than the last
facts.claim: A cup is one rounded decline and one handle; a VCP is two or more shrinking pullbacks.

facts.quote: pauses 5 to 30 sessions with no rounded decline; a cup follows a 30% run and takes at least 7 weeks to round out and handle.
facts.claim: A high tight flag pauses with no rounded decline; a cup follows a 30% run and takes 7 weeks or more.

facts.quote: Calling a 2 or 3-day dip a handle; under 5 days it is not one.
facts.claim: A named mistake: calling a 2 or 3-day dip a handle.

facts.quote: Treating the measured-move target as a sure thing; Bulkowski found only 61% reach it.
facts.claim: A named mistake: treating the measured-move target as a sure thing.

facts.quote: ch.handle_volume: dries up sharply
facts.claim: The A+ handle volume dries up sharply.

facts.quote: ch.shape_no_wild_weeks: jagged, V-ish, two violent weeks inside (ULTA)
facts.claim: A jagged cup with violent weeks inside is a B- cue.

facts.quote: ch.base_count: third or later
facts.claim: A third or later base is a B- cue.

facts.quote: A handle in the upper third of the base, within about 5% of the old high, is better.
facts.claim: A handle in the upper third, within about 5% of the old high, is better.

facts.quote: Best between 3 and 6 months (63 to 126 sessions), symmetric; very long or lopsided cups grade down.
facts.claim: Cups are best between 3 and 6 months long.

facts.quote: A wedging or deep handle, a V-shaped cup or a late base breaks out and fades back through the pivot to the stop.
facts.claim: The failure mode: a bad handle, a V or a late base fades back through the pivot to the stop.

facts.quote: A very tight trigger-day stop is cheap but fragile; the house answer is the breakeven move at 2R to 5R (B19), not a wider stop.
facts.claim: BX: a very tight stop is fragile; the answer is breakeven at 2R to 5R, not a wider stop.

facts.quote: A cup over 6 months old with the handle resting on the 50-day is a late, tired base; the base-count rule is the filter the scan cannot apply.
facts.claim: WDAY: a cup over 6 months old with the handle on the 50-day is a late, tired base.

facts.quote: Before the buy: the market reading turns Red.
facts.claim: A Red reading before the buy ends the setup.

facts.quote: Never move the stop closer to make it fit.
facts.claim: Never move the stop closer to make the size fit.

facts.quote: ch.handle_position: just above the midpoint
facts.claim: A handle just above the cup's midpoint is a B- cue.

facts.claim: ULTA: a mid-range close, a four-day fade to the stop, best 0.91R; a B- base.
BX, trigger 2019-11-26: buy 53.11, stop 52.49 (1.17%); stopped 4 sessions later at a low of 51.78.

facts.claim: BX: a 4.9x breakout reached 2.37R on day two, then one dip took the stop and the stock went on without us.

walkthroughs.title: FFIV, January 2014: the clean one
steps: FFIV, January 2014. After a 40% run, a symmetric cup, 15.6 weeks and 17.5% deep. A rounded U, not a V.
The handle: 7 days, 4.2% deep, volume at 0.74x the cup's. It sits high in the base and drifts down.
2014-01-13: it clears the handle high on 2.71x volume. Buy at market, 91.29. Stop under the day's low, 90.67.
Failure mode: a fade back through the pivot to the stop. Instead it reaches 3R the next day. A third comes off.

walkthroughs.title: MCO, September 2012: the long handle
steps: MCO, 2012. After a 40% run, a 21.6-week cup, 21.3% deep. The long, slow version of the pattern.
The handle runs 19 days and 6.7% deep. Its lows drift down, volume dries to 0.77x, and the 50-day holds.
2012-09-06: it clears the handle high on 1.6x volume. Buy at market, 40.76. Stop under the day's low, 39.73.
Failure mode: a handle that wedges up or sinks too low. This one drifted down and held. 3R in 4 sessions.

walkthroughs.title: AX, January 2026: the trims and the trail
steps: AX, 2026. A 72% run, then a 16.6-week U, 20.2% deep. The handle lasts 5 days, the IBD minimum.
2026-01-05: it clears the handle high on 1.48x volume. Buy at market, 89.22. Stop under the day's low, 86.95.
At 3R a third comes off and the stop goes to breakeven. 5R comes in about 7 weeks: another third.
Failure mode: a fade back through the pivot. AX rolled over below it after 5R. The 21-day trail sells the last third.

questions.q: In one line, what is a cup with handle?
choices: A box with a flat ceiling
A rounded U, then a dip near the top
Shrinking pullbacks, one after another
A pole that nearly doubles in weeks

wrong.A box with a flat ceiling: That is a flat base. A cup rounds down and back up, then handles.
wrong.Shrinking pullbacks, one after another: That is a VCP's contractions. A cup is one rounded decline and one handle.
wrong.A pole that nearly doubles in weeks: That is a high tight flag's pole. The cup is the rest after a smaller run.

questions.answer: A rounded U, then a dip near the top
questions.why: A rounded U, then a dip near the top. IBD: shaped like the silhouette of a tea cup viewed from the side. Zanger: the rest after a powerful advance.
questions.lesson_line: A cup is a leader's rounded rest, and the handle is the last quiet dip before the breakout.

questions.q: On a cup with handle, which level does the breakout have to trade through?
choices: The cup's lowest low in the base
The highest price in the handle
The low of the handle's last dip
The 50-day average

wrong.The cup's lowest low in the base: That is the bottom of the cup, the base's floor. The buy is at the top.
wrong.The low of the handle's last dip: The handle low is the floor of the last dip, the outer limit for the stop.
wrong.The 50-day average: The 50-day is the line the handle holds, not the trigger.

questions.answer: The highest price in the handle
questions.why: The highest price in the handle. IBD adds 10 cents to it; with a market order the 10 cents does not matter.
questions.lesson_line: Mark the handle high before the open. That is the pivot.

questions.q: On a cup breakout, the stop sits a few cents under the cup's lowest low.
questions.why: False. The stop sits a few cents under the buy day's low or the prior day's, not exactly on it. The cup's low is far too wide.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the day's low.

questions.q: A sharp V-shaped drop and rebound still counts as a cup if the depth is right.
questions.why: False. IBD: V-shaped patterns are less reliable. StockCharts: a V-shaped bottom is too sharp of a reversal to qualify.
questions.lesson_line: A cup is rounded. A V is a fast round trip, not a rest.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A handle has to last at least ___ sessions before it counts as one.
questions.why: 5. IBD: if it's shorter than five days, it's not a handle. A two or three day dip at the rim is not one yet.
questions.lesson_line: Five sessions or it is not a handle. Count them.

questions.q: Where in the base should the handle form?
choices: In the upper half of the base
Near the cup's lowest low
Anywhere, if volume is light
Below the 50-day average

wrong.Near the cup's lowest low: That is a second leg down, not a handle. Low handles fail more.
wrong.Anywhere, if volume is light: Light volume is good, but a handle in the lower half is still too low.
wrong.Below the 50-day average: A handle generally forms above the 50-day line, not under it.

questions.answer: In the upper half of the base
questions.why: In the upper half. IBD: a proper handle forms in the upper half of a base. Bulkowski says the same, and AAII keeps it out of the lower half.
questions.lesson_line: The handle forms high in the base, near the old high.

questions.q: On our card, the handle's average daily volume runs below the cup's average daily volume.
questions.why: True. The handle's volume averages below the cup's. IBD: volume should dry up, evidence that the weak holders are just about gone.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet in the handle. The sellers are running out.

questions.q: The handle high is 48.20. When do you buy?
choices: On a daily close above the right rim
In premarket, if it gaps over 48.20
As it trades through 48.20, in hours
At the handle low, before the move

wrong.On a daily close above the right rim: That is Bulkowski's later entry. We buy the trade through the handle high.
wrong.In premarket, if it gaps over 48.20: No new buys outside regular trading hours.
wrong.At the handle low, before the move: That buys inside the base with no trigger.

questions.answer: As it trades through 48.20, in hours
questions.why: As it trades through 48.20 during regular hours, at market. Bulkowski waits for a close above the rim; our trigger is the trade through the pivot.
questions.lesson_line: The trigger is the trade through the handle high. Market order, regular hours.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A cup with handle spans at least ___ weeks, the handle included.
questions.why: 7 weeks. IBD: the base must be at least seven weeks long, including the handle. Shorter is a flag or a tight range.
questions.lesson_line: Seven weeks or more. A real cup takes time to build.

questions.q: IBD wants a run up of no more than 30% before the stock turns down into the cup.
questions.why: False. IBD: the basic requirements start with a run up of at least 30%. AAII repeats it: at least 30% from the last intermediate low.
questions.lesson_line: No run, no cup. Measure the advance before the rest.

questions.q: A handle's lows rise day after day into the pivot, with no shakeout. What does IBD call that?
choices: A tight handle
A wedging handle
A shakeout
A cup without a handle

wrong.A tight handle: Tight is closes bunched together. Rising lows are a wedge.
wrong.A shakeout: A shakeout undercuts an earlier low. Rising lows never undercut anything.
wrong.A cup without a handle: A cup without a handle has no dip at all at the rim.

questions.why: A wedging handle. IBD: a wedging handle with no shakeouts is a sign to steer clear. Our card says rising lows are not a handle.
questions.lesson_line: A handle drifts down or sideways. Rising lows into the pivot are a wedge.

questions.q: On our card, one daily close under the 50-day during the handle ends the setup.
questions.why: True. A close below the 50-day during the handle ends it. IBD: a handle should generally form above the 50-day.
questions.lesson_line: The handle holds the 50-day on every close. One close under it and the cup is off.

questions.q: Before the handle starts, how close to the left-side high should the right side climb?
choices: Within about 10%
Within about 30%
At least 10% above it
Halfway back is enough

wrong.Within about 30%: That leaves the handle too low in the base. Low handles fail more.
wrong.At least 10% above it: Above the old high is already a breakout, not a right side.
wrong.Halfway back is enough: Halfway is the cup's midpoint. The handle has to sit above it.

questions.why: Within about 10%. Our card has the right side climb back to within about 10% of the left-side high before the handle starts. Zanger puts the handle about 5% below the old high and calls a lower one riskier.
questions.lesson_line: The right side comes back up near the old high. Only then does a handle start.

questions.q: By Bulkowski's count, few cup breakouts come back to the breakout price within 30 days.
questions.why: False. 62% of cup breakouts come back to the breakout price within 30 days. The day's-low stop gets tested often; that is normal.
questions.lesson_line: Expect the retest. The stop pays for it; you do not widen it.

questions.q: What is the widest our cup stop can ever sit?
choices: 8% under the buy
A few cents under the cup's low
Just under the handle low
Under the 200-day

wrong.8% under the buy: IBD's 7% to 8% is a reference, not ours.
wrong.A few cents under the cup's low: That is the whole cup's depth away. Far too wide.
wrong.Under the 200-day: The 200-day is a context line, not a stop.

questions.why: Just under the handle low, by a few cents. Below the handle low the setup has failed. Bulkowski puts his stop at the handle low.
questions.lesson_line: The handle low is the outer wall. The real stop usually sits much closer.

questions.q: On our card, a third or later cup since the last real correction is graded down.
questions.why: True. First or second base; a third or later is graded down. IBD: breakouts from late-stage bases will often blow up.
questions.lesson_line: Count the bases. Late ones get a lower grade and a smaller size.

questions.q: How many weeks with a 10% or wider range can a cup hold inside it, on our card?
choices: None at all
At most two
At most five
Any number, if it is a U

wrong.None at all: The card allows up to two. More than that is too jagged.
wrong.At most five: Five wild weeks is a jagged base. IBD wants smooth sides.
wrong.Any number, if it is a U: Shape and smoothness are both tests. Wild weeks fail the second.

questions.why: At most two. IBD: there shouldn't be many wild weekly swings of 10% to 15% or more.
questions.lesson_line: A cup is smooth. Count the violent weeks; more than two and it is not ours.

questions.q: Fill 91.29, stop 90.67. At what price does the first third come off?
questions.why: 93.15, the 3R level. One R is the fill minus the stop; add three of those to the fill. FFIV got there the next day.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open. A third comes off there.

questions.q: Our card lets a cup fall up to about 2.5 times the index's decline over the same weeks.
questions.why: True. The cup falls no more than about 2.5 times the index's decline. IBD's range is 1-1/2 to 2-1/2 times the market averages.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the cup against the market. A leader falls more than the index, but not wildly more.

questions.q: IBD allows a cup to run as deep as 50% when it forms in a bear market.
questions.why: True. IBD: in bear markets, cups can run as deep as 50%. Our card allows it only for a cup formed in a bear market.
questions.lesson_line: A deep cup is allowed only when the whole market fell hard.

questions.q: Before the buy, volume drying up through the handle ends the setup.
questions.why: False. Volume rising through the handle ends it. IBD: volume should dry up, evidence that the weak holders are just about gone.
questions.lesson_line: A loud handle means sellers are still there. Wait for quiet.

questions.q: IBD says many cups take how long to form?
choices: One to two weeks
Three to six months
Two to three years
Exactly seven weeks

wrong.One to two weeks: That is a flag's rest. A cup needs seven weeks at least.
wrong.Two to three years: IBD's longest is 65 weeks, a bit over a year.
wrong.Exactly seven weeks: Seven weeks is the minimum, not the typical length.

questions.why: Three to six months. IBD: they range from seven weeks to 65 weeks, with many forming over three to six months. Our card grades that range best.
questions.lesson_line: A real base builds slowly. Months, not days.

questions.q: Buy the breakout today?
questions.story: The handle is tight and quiet. The pivot trades through this morning. Earnings come out after tomorrow's close.
choices: Yes, it triggered over the pivot
Yes, at half the normal size
No, a report inside 3 sessions
Yes, if volume is heavy

wrong.Yes, it triggered over the pivot: The trigger fired, and the calendar still says no.
wrong.Yes, at half the normal size: Smaller is still in. The rule is no new buys.
wrong.Yes, if volume is heavy: Volume grades the day. It does not override the earnings rule.

questions.why: No. No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report. If it is still a setup after the report, it can trigger again.
questions.lesson_line: A breakout into earnings is a gap you cannot stop. Wait for the report.

questions.q: Lowest low of the prior six months 30.00, left-side high 40.50. How big was the run into the cup, in percent?
questions.why: 35%. The left-side high over the lowest low, minus one. IBD wants a run up of at least 30%; AAII says the same.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the run before the rest. A cup with no run in front of it is just a dip.

questions.q: Left-side high 80.00, the cup's lowest intraday low 58.00. How deep is the cup, in percent?
questions.why: 27.5%. The left-side high minus the cup's low, divided by the high. IBD and Zanger both measure the fall from the old high.
questions.lesson_line: Depth is high to low, divided by the high. Measure it; do not eyeball it.

questions.q: Left-side high 50.00, cup low 38.00. Where is the cup's midpoint?
questions.why: 44.00, halfway between the high and the low. IBD: the handle's own midpoint should be above the midpoint of the cup.
questions.lesson_line: Find the cup's midpoint first. The handle has to sit above it.

questions.q: Take the breakout when it comes?
questions.story: Left-side high 50.00, cup low 38.00. The right side climbs back near 49. Then a handle runs from 47.00 down to 39.50.
choices: Take it; the handle is long enough
Pass; the handle sits too low
Take it; the right side made it back

wrong.Take it; the handle is long enough: Length is one test. Position is another, and it fails.
wrong.Take it; the right side made it back: The right side did. Then the handle fell too far.

questions.answer: Pass; the handle sits too low
questions.why: Pass. The handle's midpoint, halfway between 47.00 and 39.50, sits under the cup's, halfway between 50.00 and 38.00. IBD: handles that form too low fail more.
questions.lesson_line: Check the handle's midpoint against the cup's. Too low and I pass.

questions.q: Fill 56.61, stop 55.27. How far below the fill is the stop, in percent?
questions.why: 2.37%. The fill minus the stop, divided by the fill. That sits inside the 3% the stop usually sits within. GWW's stop was 2.4%.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.

questions.q: Buy or pass?
questions.story: The handle high is 60.00. You were away for the open. At 10:30 the stock trades 62.70.
choices: Buy; the breakout is real
Buy half size
Pass; 4.5% past the pivot
Buy with a wider stop

wrong.Buy; the breakout is real: Real and too far away can both be true. The chase line is 4%.
wrong.Buy half size: Half of a chased entry is still a chased entry.
wrong.Buy with a wider stop: A wider stop to fit a late entry is the mistake, not the fix.

questions.why: Pass. 62.70 is 4.5% over the pivot, past the 4% line. Chasing costs size: the stop stays under the buy point, so the shares shrink.
questions.lesson_line: I would rather miss it than chase it. Four percent and done.

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: Four days after the breakout at 40.76, price slips back to the handle high. Your stop is 39.73.
choices: Hold; the stop stays where it is
Widen the stop to the handle low
Sell; the breakout failed
Move the stop to breakeven

wrong.Widen the stop to the handle low: Never wider. The gap rule is the one exception, and this is not a gap.
wrong.Sell; the breakout failed: A pullback to the pivot is not a failure. The stop decides.
wrong.Move the stop to breakeven: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R, not on a slide to the pivot.

questions.answer: Hold; the stop stays where it is
questions.why: Hold it. The stop only moves up, never wider. Tests of the pivot are normal: 62% of cup breakouts come back to the breakout price within 30 days.
questions.lesson_line: The retest is normal. The stop pays for it; you do not widen it.

questions.q: What now?
questions.story: You bought the breakout at 91.20 with the stop at 89.10. It closes at 89.60, back inside the handle, above your stop.
choices: Sell at the close; it failed
Hold; the stop is still the exit
Lower the stop to the handle low
Add; it is cheaper now

wrong.Sell at the close; it failed: That close is a warning, not an exit by itself. The stop decides.
wrong.Lower the stop to the handle low: The stop only moves up, never down.
wrong.Add; it is cheaper now: Full size at one price with one stop. No adding.

questions.answer: Hold; the stop is still the exit
questions.why: Hold it. A close back into the handle is a warning, not an exit by itself. The stop is the exit, and it was set before the buy.
questions.lesson_line: A weak close is a warning. The stop is the decision.

questions.q: Where is the stop now?
questions.story: You bought at 54.57 with the stop at 52.94. It gaps open at 52.40, under your stop. The first 30-minute bar's low is 52.10.
choices: Sell at the open, 52.40
52.10, the first 30-minute low
No stop until it reclaims 52.94
Get out; the gap is past 2R

wrong.Sell at the open, 52.40: The gap rule gives it the first 30 minutes. The 30-minute low decides.
wrong.No stop until it reclaims 52.94: There is always a stop. The new one is the 30-minute low.
wrong.Get out; the gap is past 2R: The 30-minute low is inside 2R here. The ceiling has not been hit.

questions.why: 52.10. A gap through the stop hands it to the first 30-minute low. That low is a loss inside 2R, so it becomes the new stop.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop is the one exception. The first 30 minutes decide.

questions.q: Bought at 53.11, stop 52.49. On day two it trades 54.58. How many R is that?
questions.why: 2.37R. The gain divided by the fill minus the stop. That is past 2R, so the breakeven move is allowed. BX got there, then one dip took the stop.
questions.lesson_line: Count in R. From 2R the stop can go to breakeven.

questions.q: Account 40,000. Risk 0.75%. Fill 40.76, stop 39.73. How many shares?
questions.why: 291. Account times risk percent, divided by the fill minus the stop, rounded down. The stop sets the size, never the other way round.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.

questions.q: Take the breakout?
questions.story: A 13-week, 20% cup. Then six days of rising lows into the pivot, and no shakeout.
choices: Take it; the cup is the right depth
Pass; a wedging handle
Take it; rising lows show strength

wrong.Take it; the cup is the right depth: The cup passes. The handle is what fails.
wrong.Take it; rising lows show strength: IBD: handles that wedge upward tend to fail.

questions.why: Pass. Rising handle lows are a wedge, not a handle. IBD: a wedging handle with no shakeouts is a sign to steer clear. This one was stopped at 0.0R.
questions.lesson_line: A handle drifts down. Rising lows into the pivot are a wedge, and I pass.

questions.q: Is it a cup with handle?
questions.story: After a 64% run the stock dips and recovers over four weeks. Then it rests seven days just under the high.
choices: Yes; the handle is long enough
No; too short to be a cup
Yes; the run before it qualifies

wrong.Yes; the handle is long enough: The handle passes. The cup is far too short.
wrong.Yes; the run before it qualifies: The run qualifies. The time does not.

questions.answer: No; too short to be a cup
questions.why: No. A cup spans at least 7 weeks, the handle included. Four weeks and a pause is too short: a flag or a short base at best.
questions.lesson_line: Count the weeks before you call it a cup. A short dip and a pause is a flag.

questions.q: What is it?
questions.story: An 8.4-week rest that dips only 6.6% from the high. Then a 9-day handle, and a breakout on heavy volume.
choices: Closer to a flat base
A shallow cup with handle
A VCP of shrinking dips

wrong.A shallow cup with handle: Too shallow for a cup. It never rounded down.
wrong.A VCP of shrinking dips: A VCP shows two or more shrinking pullbacks. This is one shallow shelf.

questions.why: Closer to a flat base. A cup is a real rounded decline; a shelf this shallow stays boxy. Treat it with the flat base's rules.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the depth first. A shallow shelf is a flat base, whatever the dip at the end looks like.

questions.q: Take it as a cup with handle?
questions.story: An 11-week drop of 22% and a straight climb back to the high. Then a 5-day handle.
choices: Take it; 22% is a normal depth
Take it; the handle is 5 days
Pass; a V, not a U

wrong.Take it; 22% is a normal depth: The depth passes. The shape fails.
wrong.Take it; the handle is 5 days: The handle is long enough, but it sits on a V.

questions.answer: Pass; a V, not a U
questions.why: Pass. That is a V, not a U. Only 12% of the cup's bars had lows in the bottom quarter, and the card needs 30%. IBD: V-shaped patterns are less reliable.
questions.lesson_line: A cup spends time at the bottom. A straight drop and a straight climb is a V.

questions.q: Does the cup with handle name apply yet?
questions.story: After a nine-week rounded base, the stock dips three days just under the rim.
choices: Yes; buy the dip
Not yet; a handle needs 5 sessions
Yes; any dip at the rim is a handle

wrong.Yes; buy the dip: A three-day dip is not a handle yet, and buying it has no trigger.
wrong.Yes; any dip at the rim is a handle: Any dip is not a handle. Five sessions is the floor.

questions.answer: Not yet; a handle needs 5 sessions
questions.why: Not yet. IBD: if it's shorter than five days, it's not a handle. Calling a 2 or 3-day dip a handle is a named mistake.
questions.lesson_line: Count the handle's days. Under five, keep waiting.

questions.q: Which handle grades higher?
questions.story: Two cups, both clean. In one, handle volume dries up sharply. In the other, it runs 0.97x the cup's average.
choices: The one that dries up sharply
The 0.97x handle
Equal; both are below the cup

wrong.The 0.97x handle: It passes, but only just. It is the weakest acceptable.
wrong.Equal; both are below the cup: Both pass the gate. Grading is about how quiet.

questions.answer: The one that dries up sharply
questions.why: The one that dries up sharply. Both are below the cup's volume, so both pass. RRC's 0.97x handle is the cue at its weakest acceptable.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet passes. Very quiet grades up.

questions.q: Your read?
questions.story: This is the stock's fourth cup since the last real correction. The shape is clean and the handle is quiet.
choices: A+, the shape is clean
Graded down, sized down
Normal size; base count is ignored

wrong.A+, the shape is clean: Clean shape does not erase the base count.
wrong.Normal size; base count is ignored: Our card counts the bases. Late ones grade down.

questions.why: Graded down, and sized down. Our card grades a third or later base down; B- or lower setups are sized down. IBD: late-stage breakouts often blow up.
questions.lesson_line: A clean cup late in the run still earns a smaller size.

questions.q: What do you take?
questions.story: The market reading is Orange. Two cups trigger the same morning. You grade one A+ and one B.
choices: Both at full size
Only the A+ cup
Neither; Orange is cash
Both at half size

wrong.Both at full size: That is Green. Orange narrows you to A+.
wrong.Neither; Orange is cash: Red is mostly cash. Orange still allows the best setups.
wrong.Both at half size: Orange is about grade, not size. The B setup waits.

questions.why: Only the A+ cup. Green is full risk; Yellow smaller and fewer; Orange only A+ setups; Red mostly cash and shorts.
questions.lesson_line: Read the market before the cup. Orange buys A+ and nothing else.

questions.q: Buy it?
questions.story: The breakout gaps up 3% over the pivot. At your fill the stock sits 12% above its 10-day average.
choices: Buy; it is inside the 4% limit
Skip; too far over the 10-day
Buy half size and keep the stop

wrong.Buy; it is inside the 4% limit: Inside the chase line, but past the stretch line. Both must pass.
wrong.Buy half size and keep the stop: Size does not fix a stretched entry.

questions.why: Skip it. A long more than 10% above its 10-day average is too stretched to buy, even inside the 4% chase line.
questions.lesson_line: Two checks at the fill: distance from the pivot and distance from the 10-day.

questions.q: Is the cup still on your list?
questions.story: In week two of the handle the stock closes under its 50-day once. The next day it recovers above it.
choices: Yes; it recovered the next day
No; it closed under the 50-day
Yes; it takes two closes

wrong.Yes; it recovered the next day: The recovery does not undo the close. The card's test is one close.
wrong.Yes; it takes two closes: One close under the 50-day in the handle is enough.

questions.why: No. A close below the 50-day during the handle ends the setup on our card. IBD: a handle should generally form above the 50-day.
questions.lesson_line: Inside the handle the 50-day holds every close. One close under and I cross it off.

questions.q: On our card, a handle is tight at the end when its last 5 closes sit within about 3% of each other.
questions.why: True. Tight at the end: the last 5 handle closes within about 3% of each other. IBD: handles should have areas of tight trading.
questions.lesson_line: Tight closes into the pivot. That is the picture I want.

questions.q: Which handle grades higher?
questions.story: Two handles, both above the cup's midpoint. One sits within 5% of the old high. The other sits just above the midpoint.
choices: The one near the old high
The one just above the midpoint
Equal; both pass the midpoint

wrong.The one just above the midpoint: It passes the gate, but it is a B- cue.
wrong.Equal; both pass the midpoint: Both pass. The grade still prefers the higher handle.

questions.answer: The one near the old high
questions.why: The one near the old high. A handle in the upper third, within about 5% of it, grades up; just above the midpoint grades down. Zanger: about 5% below the old high.
questions.lesson_line: Higher in the base is better. Just above halfway passes, and only just.

questions.q: Flat base or cup with handle?
questions.story: A leader falls 21% in a rounded U over 14 weeks. It climbs back within 4% of the high. Then it drifts 6% lower for eight days.
choices: A cup with handle
A flat base
A VCP

wrong.A flat base: Too deep and too rounded for a box.
wrong.A VCP: One rounded decline and one handle, not a series of shrinking pullbacks.

questions.why: A cup with handle. A flat base stays boxy and shallow; this one rounded down 21% and then dipped again into a handle. Zanger's cups fall 20% to 35% off the old high.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the depth and the shape. A deep rounded rest with a dip at the rim is a cup.

questions.q: Which one is the cup?
questions.story: Base A: one rounded decline, a climb back to the rim, one small dip. Base B: three pullbacks of 18%, 9% and 4%.
choices: Base A
Base B
Both are cups

wrong.Base B: Three pullbacks, each smaller than the last, is a VCP.
wrong.Both are cups: Only one has a single rounded decline and a handle.

questions.why: Base A. A cup is one rounded decline whose right side climbs back near the old high, then one handle. Base B's shrinking pullbacks are a VCP.
questions.lesson_line: Count the pullbacks. One rounded decline and a handle is a cup; shrinking swings are a VCP.

questions.q: What is it?
questions.story: The stock rose 95% in seven weeks. Then it paused nine sessions, 10% deep, just under the high.
choices: A cup with handle
A high tight flag
A flat base

wrong.A cup with handle: No rounded decline and far too short.
wrong.A flat base: A flat base is a longer rest after a smaller run.

questions.why: A high tight flag. It nearly doubled and paused a few weeks with no rounded decline. A cup follows a 30% run and takes at least 7 weeks.
questions.lesson_line: Doubled and paused is a flag. Ran and rounded for months is a cup.

questions.q: Was that loss a mistake?
questions.story: A 16-week, 19% cup after a 76% run, an 8-day handle. You bought 260.96, stop 257.75. It closed mid-range and faded four days to your stop.
choices: No; a planned loss at the stop
Yes; the stop needed more room
Yes; sell on any mid-range close

wrong.Yes; the stop needed more room: The stop only moves up. More room is a bigger loss, not a fix.
wrong.Yes; sell on any mid-range close: A weak close is a warning, not an exit by itself.

questions.answer: No; a planned loss at the stop
questions.why: No. The stop is the exit, and the loss was the plan. A cup with a 10%-range week and heavy-volume days grades B-, and a B- base earns a smaller size.
questions.lesson_line: A loss at the stop is the system working. The grade decides how big it is.

questions.q: What does our rule allow now?
questions.story: A 10-week, 18% cup with a 5-day handle breaks out on 4.9x volume. You bought 53.11, stop 52.49. On day two it reaches 2.37R.
choices: Widen the stop for room
Move the stop to breakeven
Sell it all at 2.37R
Add to the position

wrong.Widen the stop for room: Never wider. A tight stop is answered with breakeven.
wrong.Sell it all at 2.37R: The first trim is a third at 3R, not everything at 2.37R.
wrong.Add to the position: Full size at one price with one stop. No adding.

questions.why: Moving the stop to breakeven. B19 allows it from 2R to 5R. BX's tight stop was taken by one dip on day five, and the stock went on without us.
questions.lesson_line: A tight stop is cheap but fragile. From 2R, breakeven protects it; a wider stop never does.

questions.q: Next morning it trades under your stop. What do you do?
questions.story: A 30-week, 23% cup; the 8-day handle rests on the 50-day. You bought 273.63, stop 266.70. The day closed 270.71, low in its range.
choices: Out at the stop, as planned
Hold; the cup is still valid
Lower the stop under the handle

wrong.Hold; the cup is still valid: The stop is the exit. The cup's shape does not move it.
wrong.Lower the stop under the handle: The stop only moves up, never down.

questions.answer: Out at the stop, as planned
questions.why: Out at the stop, as planned. A cup over 6 months old with the handle resting on the 50-day is a late, tired base. If it sets up again, that is a new trade.
questions.lesson_line: Out at the stop. A new trigger later is a new trade with its own stop.

questions.q: Did you break a rule?
questions.story: The pivot is 72.58. It gaps open and you fill at 74.57. It never trades above your fill, and the next day takes the 73.36 stop.
choices: Yes; never buy a gap open
No; inside 4%, a planned loss
Yes; the stop was too tight

wrong.Yes; never buy a gap open: No rule bans a gap fill inside 4% of the pivot.
wrong.Yes; the stop was too tight: The stop sat under the day's low by the rule.

questions.why: No. A fill 2.7% over the pivot is inside the 4% chase line, and the stop was the exit. A gap it cannot build on is the first sign the answer is no.
questions.lesson_line: A planned loss is not a mistake. A gap that cannot build is the warning.

questions.q: IBD's 7% to 8% loss limit is the stop we use on a cup breakout.
questions.why: False. IBD's 7% to 8% is a reference, not ours. Our stop sits a few cents under the buy day's or prior day's low, usually within about 3%.
questions.lesson_line: Our loss is the day's range, not a fixed percent of the price.

questions.q: What happens to the last third?
questions.story: You bought 89.22, stop 86.95. A third came off at 3R and a third at 5R. Weeks later it rolls over and closes under the 21-day.
choices: Held until it closes under the pivot
Sold on that close under the 21-day
Held; the stop is at breakeven
Added to on the dip

wrong.Held until it closes under the pivot: The trail is the rising average, not the pivot.
wrong.Held; the stop is at breakeven: Breakeven guards the trade. The trail sells the last third.
wrong.Added to on the dip: No adding. The plan only sells from here.

questions.answer: Sold on that close under the 21-day
questions.why: Sold on that close. The last third trails the 10-day for a fast mover or the 21-day for a steadier one. AX rolled over below the pivot after 5R.
questions.lesson_line: Two thirds banked, one on the trail. The close under the line is the exit.

questions.q: Where are the stop and the first trim?
questions.story: A 15.6-week cup and a quiet 7-day handle. It clears the handle high on 2.71x volume; you fill at 91.29. The lower of that day's and the prior day's low is 90.72.
choices: Stop 90.72; a third at 2R
Stop 90.67; a third at 3R
Stop at the handle low; out at 5R

wrong.Stop 90.72; a third at 2R: The stop sits a few cents under the low, and the first trim is 3R.
wrong.Stop at the handle low; out at 5R: The handle low is the outer limit, not the stop.

questions.why: Stop 90.67, a few cents under 90.72, and a third off at 3R. FFIV reached 3R the next day.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, stop, trim, trail. Write it before the open.

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the day before the breakout. Judge the handle's place in the base and its drift. Take it or pass.
choices: Take it; a high, quiet handle
Pass; the handle sits too low
Pass; the handle wedges up

wrong.Pass; the handle sits too low: It sits well above the cup's midpoint.
wrong.Pass; the handle wedges up: Its lows drift down, not up.

questions.answer: Take it; a high, quiet handle
questions.why: Take it. The handle sits high and quiet above the cup's midpoint. A symmetric cup and a quiet handle; it broke out the next day on 2.7x volume.
questions.lesson_line: Check the handle's place in the base before anything else. High and quiet is the picture.

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the day before it trades through the handle high. Look at the handle's lows. Take it or pass.
choices: Take it; the cup is 20% deep
Pass; the handle's lows rise
Take it; it is near the highs

wrong.Take it; the cup is 20% deep: The cup is fine. The handle wedges up.
wrong.Take it; it is near the highs: Near the highs is the place. The wedge is the problem.

questions.why: Pass. Six days of rising lows into the pivot is a wedging handle with no shakeout. It never traded above its fill before the stop (best 0.0R).
questions.lesson_line: The cup can be fine and the handle still wrong. Rising lows, I pass.

questions.q: What do you do with the breakout?
questions.story: Your best cup sits a few cents under the pivot. Overnight the market reading turns Red.
choices: Buy it; A+ cups trade anywhere
No new long; mostly cash
Buy half size

wrong.Buy it; A+ cups trade anywhere: Red is mostly cash. The setup is off.
wrong.Buy half size: Half size is still a new long in a Red market.

questions.why: No new long. A Red reading before the buy ends the setup; in a Red market we hold mostly cash, plus shorts below the 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: The best cup in a Red market is a cup. Sit on your hands.

questions.q: How many do you buy on day one?
questions.story: A correction just ended and the reading turned Green. Six leaders in one group show cups at their pivots.
choices: All six; Green is full risk
A few; add as they work
None; wait a month

wrong.All six; Green is full risk: Green allows full risk, but after a correction you start with a few.
wrong.None; wait a month: This is the moment the best cups come. Start small, not never.

questions.answer: A few; add as they work
questions.why: A few, adding more only as the first ones work. Zanger: the best cups come at the beginning of a market move after a good correction.
questions.lesson_line: Green after a correction: a few positions first. Let the winners earn the next ones.

questions.q: Can you hold through the report?
questions.story: Your cup long is up 5.6R. Earnings come out tomorrow after the close.
choices: Yes; it is up past 5R
No; always sell before a report
Only if it is up 10R

wrong.No; always sell before a report: The rule allows a hold when the trade is up 5R.

questions.why: Yes, you may. We hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R, and this one is past it. Under 5R it would be sold first.
questions.lesson_line: Earnings is a gap you cannot stop. Five R buys the ticket.

questions.q: How do we take profits on a cup winner?
choices: At the cup's measured-move target
All of it at a 20% to 25% gain
In R: thirds at 3R and 5R, trail
At the old high

wrong.At the cup's measured-move target: Treating the target as a sure thing is a named mistake.
wrong.All of it at a 20% to 25% gain: That is IBD's general rule, not ours.
wrong.At the old high: The old high is the pivot area. That is where the trade starts.

questions.answer: In R: thirds at 3R and 5R, trail
questions.why: In R: a third at 3R, a third at 5R, then trail the last third. IBD takes most profits at 20% to 25%; Bulkowski's target is no sure thing.
questions.lesson_line: Sell partials into strength, in R. Targets are guesses; trims are rules.

questions.q: On our card, a handle under a week old with no breakout is stale.
questions.why: False. A handle past about 6 weeks, 30 sessions, with no breakout is getting stale, and the card takes it off.
questions.lesson_line: A handle is a short pause. Months of it is a stall.

questions.q: Take it?
questions.story: In a normal market, a leader's cup fell 42% in a rounded U. Then a tidy 8-day handle formed near the high.
choices: Take it; the 8-day handle is tidy
Pass; too deep for a normal market
Take it; IBD allows cups to run 50%

wrong.Take it; the 8-day handle is tidy: The handle passes. The cup is far too deep.
wrong.Take it; IBD allows cups to run 50%: Only in a bear market. Here the market is normal.

questions.answer: Pass; too deep for a normal market
questions.why: Pass. Deeper than 35% outside a bear market ends the setup. IBD allows 50% only in bear markets; Zanger's cups run 20% to 35% off the old high.
questions.lesson_line: A tidy handle does not fix a cup that fell too far.

questions.q: Which one is never allowed?
questions.story: The breakout fills at 48.60. The buy day's low sits at 46.40, about 4.5% under your fill.
choices: Skip the trade; the stop is wide
Pull the stop in to 3% to fit
Wait for a tighter spot

wrong.Skip the trade; the stop is wide: Skipping is always allowed when the honest stop does not fit.
wrong.Wait for a tighter spot: Waiting is always allowed. No rule makes you buy this breakout. Pulling the stop in is not allowed.

questions.answer: Pull the stop in to 3% to fit
questions.why: Pulling the stop in to fit. Stop first; the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
questions.lesson_line: You never pick a size and back-fit a stop inside the noise.

questions.q: What does our rule say?
questions.story: Weeks after the breakout your cup winner runs three straight up days. Two of them gap up overnight, on rising volume.
choices: Sell a big part into it
Add; it is breaking out again
Do nothing; let the trail decide

wrong.Add; it is breaking out again: No adding, and a burst is where we sell, not buy.
wrong.Do nothing; let the trail decide: The trail handles the slow exit. A climax is a chance to sell into strength.

questions.answer: Sell a big part into it
questions.why: Sell a big part into it, a judgment call. That is the shape of Bracco's parabolic burst: up days, gap ups, range expansion and rising volume.
questions.lesson_line: A climax run is a gift. Sell a big part into it.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: We buy leaders: an RS rating of ___ or more, in one of the strongest groups.
questions.why: 80. Our rulebook buys leaders with an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups. Parabolic and mean-reversion trades are the exceptions.
questions.lesson_line: Buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in a strong group.

questions.q: Which cup do you take?
questions.story: Two clean cups trigger the same morning. One stock has an RS rating of 92 in a top group. The other has a rating of 55 in a weak group.
choices: The 92 cup in the strong group
The 55 cup, since it has more room
Both, each at half the usual size
The one with the tighter handle

wrong.The 55 cup, since it has more room: A weak rating in a weak group is a laggard. We buy leaders, 80 or more.
wrong.Both, each at half the usual size: Half size does not fix a laggard. The 55 cup fails the leader test.
wrong.The one with the tighter handle: Handle tightness grades a cup. It does not replace the leader test.

questions.answer: The 92 cup in the strong group
questions.why: The 92 cup. We buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups. A rating of 55 in a weak group is a laggard.
questions.lesson_line: A clean chart on a laggard is still a laggard. Buy the leader.

questions.q: What does our rule say?
questions.story: A stock grows sales and earnings every quarter. Its cup is a sharp V, with a 5-day dip at the rim. Price trades through the handle high.
choices: Pass; the chart comes first
Buy; the growth outweighs the shape
Buy half size and trim fast
Buy a starter, add after earnings

wrong.Buy; the growth outweighs the shape: We prefer growth, but the chart comes first. V-shaped patterns are less reliable.
wrong.Buy half size and trim fast: Small size does not fix a failed shape. The chart comes first.
wrong.Buy a starter, add after earnings: The V fails the chart test now. We do not buy a weak chart on growth alone.

questions.why: Pass; the chart comes first. We prefer growing sales and earnings, but a V-shaped cup fails the chart, whatever the growth.
questions.lesson_line: Growth is a plus. The chart decides first.

questions.q: A clean cup breakout is fine to buy even when price sits under its 200-day average.
questions.why: False. Our rule: no longs below the 200-day, unless it is a parabolic long. A cup with a handle is not a parabolic long.
questions.lesson_line: No long under the 200-day. A tidy cup does not change that.

questions.q: The cup is clean and price trades through the 31.40 pivot. The 200-day average is 33.10. Which rule decides this?
choices: No longs under the 200-day average
No chasing more than 4% over the pivot
No new buys within 3 days of earnings
A stop that only moves up

wrong.No chasing more than 4% over the pivot: The buy is at the pivot, so there is no chase. The 200-day is the issue.
wrong.No new buys within 3 days of earnings: Nothing here mentions a report. The 200-day average decides this one.
wrong.A stop that only moves up: That rule matters after the buy. It does not decide whether to buy.

questions.why: No longs under the 200-day average. The pivot is 31.40 and the 200-day is 33.10, so price sits under it. Skip the cup.
questions.lesson_line: Check the 200-day before the pivot. Under it, no long.

questions.q: A cup stock averages 600,000 shares a day at $28. How many millions of dollars does it trade a day?
questions.why: 16.8 million. That is under our floor of $20 million traded a day, so we skip it, however clean the cup.
questions.lesson_line: Price times shares is dollars traded. We need $20 million a day.

questions.q: A $7 stock that trades $40 million a day passes our liquidity floor.
questions.why: False. We trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. At $7 it fails the price test.
questions.lesson_line: Both tests count: $10 a share and $20 million a day.

questions.q: A stock averages 250,000 shares a day. Under our volume rule, what is the most shares we may own?
questions.why: 2,500 shares. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume. One percent of 250,000 is 2,500.
questions.lesson_line: Cap every position at 1% of average daily volume.

questions.q: How many shares do you buy?
questions.story: The risk math allows 6,000 shares of a cup breakout. The stock averages 300,000 shares a day.
choices: 3,000 shares
6,000 shares
4,500 shares
1,500 shares

wrong.6,000 shares: The risk math sets a size, but this is over 1% of average daily volume. The volume cap wins.
wrong.4,500 shares: Still over 1% of average daily volume. Trim it to the cap.
wrong.1,500 shares: That is safe but half the cap. The 1% rule is a ceiling, not a target.

questions.why: 3,000 shares. The risk math allows 6,000, but we never own more than 1% of average daily volume. One percent of 300,000 is 3,000.
questions.lesson_line: Size is the smaller of the risk math and the volume cap.

questions.q: On our card, the down weeks on a cup's left side roughly match the up weeks on its right side.
questions.why: True. IBD says the down weeks on the left should roughly match the up weeks on the right. A lopsided cup grades lower.
questions.lesson_line: A good cup is symmetric: weeks down on the left, weeks up on the right.

questions.q: A cup takes 8 weeks to fall and 2 weeks to climb back. What does the symmetry cue say?
choices: Lopsided, so it grades lower
Fine, depth is all that counts
Strong, a fast recovery is best
Fine, if the handle is quiet

wrong.Fine, depth is all that counts: Depth is one test. IBD also wants the down and up weeks to roughly match.
wrong.Strong, a fast recovery is best: A rebound that fast is lopsided, close to a V, and V-shaped patterns are less reliable.
wrong.Fine, if the handle is quiet: A quiet handle is a separate cue. It does not fix a lopsided cup.

questions.why: Lopsided, so it grades lower. IBD wants the down weeks on the left to roughly match the up weeks on the right. 8 against 2 is far apart.
questions.lesson_line: Count the weeks down and the weeks up. They should roughly match.

questions.q: AAII says a typical handle forms over about one to four weeks.
questions.why: True. AAII says a handle typically forms over about one to four weeks. StockCharts says ideally within one to four weeks. Our card agrees.
questions.lesson_line: A typical handle runs one to four weeks.

questions.q: What does our card do with it?
questions.story: A cup has a quiet handle. Its lows drift down and every close holds above the 50-day. It has now run 24 sessions with no breakout.
choices: Grade it down; keep it on the list
Drop it; the handle is stale
Grade it up; a long handle is best
Buy now, before it gets older

wrong.Drop it; the handle is stale: Stale starts past about 30 sessions. This handle is at 24.
wrong.Grade it up; a long handle is best: Long handles grade down. A typical handle runs 1 to 4 weeks.
wrong.Buy now, before it gets older: The buy is the trade through the handle high. No trade, no buy.

questions.answer: Grade it down; keep it on the list
questions.why: Grade it down; keep it on the list. A handle over about 22 sessions is graded down. It goes stale only past about 30 sessions.
questions.lesson_line: Handles over about 22 sessions grade down. Past about 30 they are stale.

questions.q: Handle high 50.00, handle low 47.50. How deep is the handle, in percent?
questions.why: 5.0%. Depth is the fall from the handle's own high. Our card calls 8% or less better, and about 5% best.
questions.lesson_line: Handle depth is the fall from its own high. Shallower grades higher.

questions.q: Which handle grades higher on our card?
questions.story: Two clean cups, each with a quiet handle that drifts down. One handle is 4% deep. The other is 11% deep.
choices: The 4% handle
The 11% handle
They grade the same

wrong.The 11% handle: A deeper handle gives back more. Our card grades shallower handles higher.
wrong.They grade the same: Depth counts on our card: 8% or less is better, and about 5% is best.

questions.why: The 4% handle. Our card grades shallower handles higher: 8% or less is better, and about 5% is best.
questions.lesson_line: Shallow handles grade higher. Aim for 8% or less.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: IBD says a handle should generally form ___ the 50-day or 10-week moving average.
questions.why: Above. IBD says a handle should generally form above the 50-day or 10-week moving averages. Our card is stricter: no close under the 50-day.
questions.lesson_line: A good handle holds above the 50-day.

questions.q: What does our rule say about that plan?
questions.story: You bought a cup breakout at 54.57 with the stop at 52.94. You plan to watch the screen and sell by hand if it breaks 52.94.
choices: Enter the stop as a real order
Fine, if you stay at the screen
Fine, a stop this tight is safe
Set a price alert and sell by hand

wrong.Fine, if you stay at the screen: Screens fail and gaps jump. A stop kept in your head is not a stop.
wrong.Fine, a stop this tight is safe: A tight stop does not make a mental one safe. The order goes in with the broker.
wrong.Set a price alert and sell by hand: An alert is a reminder, not an order. Every position has a real stop order.

questions.answer: Enter the stop as a real order
questions.why: Enter the stop as a real order. Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head.
questions.lesson_line: A stop in your head is not a stop. Put the order in.

questions.q: Our stop is a real order with the broker, and it only moves up.
questions.why: True. Every position has a real stop order with the broker. The stop only moves up, never down or wider. The gap rule is the one exception.
questions.lesson_line: A real order with the broker, and it only moves up.

questions.q: What do you do with the first third?
questions.story: You bought at 91.29 with the stop at 90.67, so 3R is 93.15. The next morning the stock opens at 94.20.
choices: Sell that third at the open
Wait for a pullback to 93.15
Skip it and wait for 5R
Sell it at the close instead

wrong.Wait for a pullback to 93.15: A gap can fill and hand the gain back. The rule is to take it at the open.
wrong.Skip it and wait for 5R: The hard rule is a third at 3R. Waiting for 5R skips the trim.
wrong.Sell it at the close instead: The rule says at the open. Waiting until the close adds risk for no reason.

questions.answer: Sell that third at the open
questions.why: Sell that third at the open. If a stock opens above a trim level, we take that trim at the open. Here 3R was 93.15.
questions.lesson_line: A gap over the trim level means you take the trim at the open.

questions.q: If a stock opens above 3R, we wait for it to fall back to 3R before we trim.
questions.why: False. If a stock opens above a trim level, we take that trim at the open. A gap can fill and give the gain back.
questions.lesson_line: Opens above a trim level: take that trim at the open.

questions.q: Before the buy, a quiet handle is still off the list if its midpoint sits below the cup's midpoint.
questions.why: True. The handle's midpoint must sit above the cup's midpoint. Under it, the handle is too low, and the setup is off before the buy.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet is not enough. The handle must sit above the cup's midpoint.

questions.q: Before the buy, what do those lows make of the handle?
questions.story: A clean cup, then a 6-session handle. Its lows run 47.0, 47.2, 47.4, 47.6, 47.9 and 48.3. Volume is quiet.
choices: A wedge, which fails more often
A tight handle, which grades best
A shakeout, which is a good sign
A V shape, which fails the cup

wrong.A tight handle, which grades best: Tight closes are a separate cue. These lows climb, so the line trends up.
wrong.A shakeout, which is a good sign: No low undercuts an earlier one. The lows climb every session into the pivot.
wrong.A V shape, which fails the cup: A V describes the cup's shape, not the handle's lows.

questions.answer: A wedge, which fails more often
questions.why: A wedge, which fails more often. A straight line through those lows slopes up. IBD: wedging handles have a higher failure rate.
questions.lesson_line: Fit a line through the handle's lows. It must slope flat or down.

questions.q: A 4-session dip under the rim becomes a handle if the breakout comes on heavy volume.
questions.why: False. If it's shorter than five days, it's not a handle. Volume does not change that, and the setup is off before the buy.
questions.lesson_line: Under five sessions is not a handle, whatever the volume.

Base count: this card grades a third or later base down (ch.base_count, gate false) while the SET.07 pilot keyed a fourth flat base as a pass. q41 keys 'graded down, sized down' (c19, c35, D38). The two units should agree once the owner rules; the glossary's base_count entry also says graded down, not banned.
UNITS-method SET.09 says 'mark the handle high and the cup low on a weekly chart'. The weekly chart is D-012 (pending), so the unit never says weekly in a key.

UNITS-method SET.09 drills 'reject a handle that forms in the lower half'. The card's gate is IBD's midpoint test (the handle's midpoint above the cup's midpoint), which q26, q27 and q57 teach; AAII's 'not into the lower half' is quoted beside it (a01).

WDAY 2021-09-22: dossier section 12 says the breakout day 'closed near its high'; section 13 and the card say it closed in the lower third of its range (close 270.71 against a 273.63 buy). q52 follows section 13 and the card.

ULTA 2016-12-16: dossier section 12 says two heavy-volume 10%-range weeks; section 13 and the card say one 10%-range week (the ceiling is two). q50 cites section 13 (d21) and the card's B- row (c34) and never counts the weeks.

Handle and the 50-day: our card's test is one close (ch.inv_close_under_50, the dossier's proposal); IBD says only 'should generally form above'. SET.07's flat base allows a brief shakeout under the 50-day (80% of closes). q12 and q44 key the cup card's one-close test as ours.

Prior trend: the card's 120-session window is its own proposal (the glossary's canonical window is 65 sessions). q10 and q24 key only the 30%, which IBD and AAII both state; AAII 2015 repeats O'Neil, so it is not independent agreement.

Throwbacks: the 62% is Bulkowski's measured throwback rate as the card states it (c17); the dossier's section 4 holds his page's statistics, which were not quoted here (the brief allows quotes from section 3 only).
Breakeven: q33 and q51 say the stop 'may' go to breakeven from 2R (B19: 2R to 5R, ideally); the card's default is at the first trim. Neither key makes breakeven before 3R a must.
The handle-low stop: Bulkowski's stop is the handle low (b04). Our card keeps it only as the outer limit (ch.stop_outer_limit, proposed); q15 and q54 teach it that way.

The dossier's example numbers (d1) are a Tier 3 repo source read off our own daily bars by the research scan (sections 12 and 13); the owner has not reviewed them (D-007). The walk-throughs, the stories and the two chart items depend on them.

The criteria card (c1) is cited as Tier 3 for its proposed criteria (the shape tests, the handle tests, the stop's outer limit, the invalidations, the lookalike tells). Those are the dossier's proposals, not owner rulings; every question keyed on them carries house: true and the owner's review is the gate.

Walk-through fills: the scan filled at the pivot plus a cent, or at the open when it gapped over the pivot, and stopped 5 cents under the lower of the trigger day's and the prior day's low. A live market order fills a little differently. The handle high is not printed in the dossier for FFIV, MCO or AX, so the walk-throughs say 'clears the handle high' and give the fill.

Chart items: q57 FFIV asof 2014-01-10 (the Friday before the 2014-01-13 trigger) is the 'take it'; q58 AAPL asof 2021-04-28 (the day before the 2021-04-29 near-miss date) is the 'pass'. The keys rest on the dossier's reads (d02, d30), not on reading the picture. AAPL also appears as a winner (2021-11-17); only the April 2021 chart is shown.
IBD's profit rule (take most at 20% to 25%) and the measured-move target are contrasted in q62 and never taught as ours; our trims are B19 and E51.
Bulkowski's site carries a notice against using it to train AI systems; only short quotes with links are used, as the dossier did.
The short mirror, the inverted cup (dossier 8.6), is not taught (D-001).

Cold check 2026-11-10: 67 pass (6 fixed), 0 fix, 2 cut. Cut: q35 (same AAPL wedge as q58), q52 (a third 'the stop is the exit' story after q31 and q50). Fixed in place: q13 (why now leads with the card's 10%), q38 (24-word sentence), q50 (why no longer says a no-mistake loss 'should have been' smaller), q57 (the question gave its own answer), q58 (0.0R wording), q65 (a wrong note leaned on pending ch.stop_width). No key rests on a pending-owner number: q25, q47, q64 use depths that are inside or outside every ch.cup_depth option; q02 mentions IBD's 10 cents only inside ch.pivot. The owner should look first at: (1) ch.base_count against the flat-base pilot (q16, q41); (2) q30, which reuses MCO's buy and stop in a made-up story while MCO itself hit 3R in 4 sessions; (3) q42, which reads the Orange guide (F65, a guide under A10) as a rule. The hidden-ticker charts (q57, q58) were not viewed; the numbers match the dossier.
